utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, and good morning -- good afternoon to you, too. Please take a seat. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic. I appear for Mr. Naser Oric together with Mr. John Jones. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team. Before I address matters which are leftovers from yesterday, are there any preliminary matters that you would like to raise? I see none. So I want to make sure that the witness is informed that it will take some time before we bring him in because we need to address a procedural matter which may be more than procedural which has got nothing to do with him. You will recall, Mr. Wubben, that yesterday Mr. Jones -- or rather, the Defence gave advance notice of a Defence motion regarding alleged prosecutorial non-compliance with Rule 68. And at the time we were given, like you were, a courtesy copy. Eventually the -- we received the formal document which had been filed in the registry, and I made it known to you that first thing today we would look towards you and expect your reaction on the alleged non-compliance. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I requested Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio to do the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours have obviously read the submission -- the motion -- the Defence motion. The -- I think the time-line needs to be given to you so that you can assess the impact of this complaint of non-disclosure. First of all, the substance of the motion that seems to be concerned with Annex A, that's the article "to live together, to live better," or "how I killed Croats and Muslims." The other piece of evidence, Annex C, the headline "I keep dreaming about snakes drinking blood" appears to be a vehicle to demonstrate to you how we knew about this paramilitary quite some time ago and that therefore we have failed to produce to you -- to the Defence the Annex A although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment, please, Mr. Di Fazio. Do you agree with the way this has been presented so far, Mr. Jones, because yesterday you did start and dealt with one document more than you did with the other but you did not distinguish the two as regards the alleged importance. So I want your position -- I would like to have your position on this before Mr. Di Fazio proceeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact, as regards non-disclosure equally Annex C should have been disclosed for the same reason. Mr. Di Fazio is right that the -- our compliant focuses primarily on Annex C, but I wouldn't confine it to annex it. It certainly would include Annex C as well. But he's right that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Annex A, not Annex C. Annex A.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, focuses on Annex A but Annex C equally the complaint can be made. And it does establish the time-line that in the sense obviously the date is 1997, and we have the spokesperson of the Tribunal saying that the Office of the Prosecutor knew about the confession of this very volunteer. So it goes to the fact that this is something which is in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution which is relevant to Rule 68(A) [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Mr. Di Fazio, you have heard what Mr. Jones said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think you can proceed, assuming that that is what the complaint seeks to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, the failed -- alleged failed disclosure covers both documents but obviously more emphasis is being laid on Annex A rather than on C.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, Annex C in the Prosecution's submission doesn't come within the category of documents covered by Rule 68. So I will make that submission. If you just flick your eyes through it, you'll see that it's a publication called Focus, which I understand is a well-publicised and well-known document. The man being interviewed, Misic, talks about his arrest by the Serbian secret police, or rather the article does, and then it continues where he was arrested. Then it continues under the heading "they had better kill me." And then describes the lurid content of the document and what he's about to talk about. And then he continues what I gather are the words of this man -- this man -- I'll call him TOP since that's his nickname and that's easier to refer to. And he says that he fought for them on the Vukovar battlefield and in Bosnia on the banks of the Drina. Now, the fact that he fought in Drina is not exculpatory evidence, cannot be exculpatory evidence, that bold fact alone. And then he goes on to say he doesn't want to end up like Albanians. I'm looking at page -- the ERN ending 66. He -- lurid language about slaughtering pigs. He talks about fighting with Croats. He talks about being a Serbian volunteer. He talks about events in Vukovar, not the area that our indictment is concerned with. Then he says: "In Bosnia I was on the bank of the Drina, we held the corridor from Skelani to Bratunac. We had everything, food, weaponry, ammunition. We fought about Muslims, poor and hungry lot. We guarded Serbian villages from their intrusion and that there were ambushes and that they would go to cleanse Muslim village in the hills." There's no indication of where these areas are in particular that he's talking about, other than the general area of the Drina, and far more importantly, of course, it is accepted by the Prosecution that Serb forces committed bad acts in the area of the Drina and has never been contested by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll interrupt you again here. But it does say "we held the corridor from Skelani to Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, well, that Serb action is engaged in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does describe the Muslims as a poor and hungry lot. It does state that the Serbian forces had everything, food, weaponry, and ammunition, which seems to be in contrast with the situation prevailing amongst the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does say that Serbian villages were being guarded from their intrusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which may, according to the Defence, at least as I understood Mr. Jones yesterday, go beyond the -- the tenuous and particular description of these villages being defended by village guards rather than by the armed forces of the Serbs. It does acknowledge that the Muslims were coming down from various places to steal food in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and, Your Honour, in case the Prosecution isn't aware, Bjelovac and Fakovici are between Bratunac and Skelani, so merely to assist Mr. Di Fazio, because perhaps he seems not to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio definitely knows where Fakovici is. He wasn't with us when we went there, but I don't doubt for a moment that he knows exactly the topographical layout of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution says that none of these issues that are in that particular paragraph are matters that have been challenged by the -- by the Defence -- by the Prosecution. The guarding of villages by this particular grouping of paramilitaries, if -- there's no grouping defined or outlined in this particular document as far as I can see -- none of the villages that are mentioned in the indictment are identified here. So the exculpatory nature of this document, if it has any, is considerably diminished by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The rest of the document, in the Prosecution's submission, doesn't contain anything that could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- exculpatory. There's a reference to decapitated bodies and we were the Territorial Defence and the special units coming long in red berets and camouflage uniforms. It's not clear what the area they are talking about. Reading it in a favourable way to the Defence, one can assume that -- one can say that he's probably talking about the Drina area. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if that is the case, even if it's not clear, do you have the right to say, This is not, clear even though the previous paragraph mentions the Drina and the area from Skelani to Bratunac, and then decide, We don't consider this as exculpatory, therefore we don't disclose it? And it's not just exculpatory material that you -- which would be the reason for -- for disclosure. It could also be if it gives the Defence sufficient material within which to counter some of your own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And attack their credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may I -- I'm frankly horrified from what I'm hearing from the Prosecution and I'll respond in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will give you that opportunity later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's for clarification. This is an exceedingly pedantic analysis, I submit. The clarification I would request is, is Mr. Di Fazio saying that the Prosecution considered whether to disclose this and they looked at this material and they had a meeting and they thought about it and they decided not to it, or is he merely reacting today, having been taken surprise by this document and now he's trying to wheedle his way out by finding how maybe it's unclear. Is he saying this something they've done in the past, this review, or is he doing it now for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that observation, because ultimately I was going to come up with that observation myself, depending, of course, on what explanation was going to be forthcoming from the Prosecution. So, yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution hasn't reviewed this document until this particular motion was made, until this particular motion was delivered by the Defence. So I'm now reacting to the motion that has been filed yesterday and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say "the Prosecution" it means the whole team basically? This is what you're saying? The whole team in this case as it was in the beginning up to today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it changed composition --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- from the pre-trial stage to what it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. If the document had been -- if we had come across it, it would have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there an explanation why on earth such an important document, particularly as Annex A --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I was going to turn to Annex A if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then please, because that's what we want to hear most.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Annex A, if Your Honours please, is -- what you have in the motion is an English translation -- I've asked for inquiries to be made as to what is in the possession of the OTP. And what is, as I understand it -- this is a Defence translation. What is in the possession of the OTP is a document, is a magazine document, or it appears to be a magazine document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's this, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- or publication -- yes, that's right. And that is the document that's actually in the possession of the OTP. I've been unable to get anyone to bring up an English translation from our computer that -- to indicate that we've translated that particular document. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment. Do you confirm that this is your own translation, not a translation that was handed to you by the Prosecution, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we had to translate it ourselves to help the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you have a confirmation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The B/C/S version of the document, if Your Honours please, was obtained in March of 2002 from -- from Bosnia and it was entered into the -- into our computer system, MIF'd, in -- again in March of 2002. In fact, it may have been seized somewhat earlier than that, but it was actually MIF'd or put into the system in March of 2002. So the suggestion that this document has been in the possession of the Prosecution for any longer than that is not correct, if that suggestion is being made. In any event, the position is it's been in our possession since March of 2002. If Your Honours please, EDS, the Electronic Disclosure Suite, was set up and functioning in November of 2003. So that's a year and some months after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's almost two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's almost two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In this particular case, Defence counsel were appointed in -- around early and mid-2003 and obtained their passwords and user names and were therefore in a position to access material held on EDS as from November of 2003. Now, I've caused inquiries to be made to check when this particular document was in fact placed on EDS. I understand from what I've been told, from the number and the nature of the document, that it was available -- it was probably available -- would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It was available, the document itself was available on the 9th of the June, 2004. So that's the time that the Defence would have first had access to that document. I understand that the document itself contains -- it's not a -- it can be searched itself. If you type in "Fakovici" and search, you should be able to locate this particular document, and I don't know as I speak what title it had in any list or index of documents in the EDS. So the effect of that is that since June of 2004, if my information is correct, the Defence had had access to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I wonder if you are aware of the consequences of what you're saying. Because if the Defence had access to that document on EDS, equally the Prosecution had access to it. And the onus of disclosing material which is exculpatory or which falls within the parameters of Rule 68 falls on the Prosecution and not on the Defence. So if you had the equal opportunity of accessing that document way back in 2004, if not before, and assuming for the sake of the argument that it does contain exculpatory or Rule 68 material, why didn't you disclose it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is what we want to hear. It's not the availability of it on EDS because that prescinds from the obligation -- or the obligation that you have under Rule 68 prescinds over the availability of the document in -- on the electronic data system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It can't assist the Prosecution in terms of the initial -- any initial breach of Rule 68. It can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Excuse me. The Prosecution has got an unlimited responsibility and obligation under Rule 68(i) to disclose to the Defence all material that is Rule 68(i) material, that is either mitigating, exculpatory, or which goes to the credibility of witnesses, and so on and so forth. That carries with it a parallel obligation on our part to continually check for exculpatory material or Rule 68 material. And the moment you come across such material, you need to disclose it. You have a sacrosanct obligation to disclose it. And it's no excuse to say, Yeah, but now, you know, we've put everything on the EDS system and if they want, they can find it out themselves. That's no excuse. We are not going to tolerate it. We have closed a blind eye, or if not a blind eye, we closed one eye, sometimes even both, when it was cases of non-disclosure which did not carry that much consequence or which were not that significant, although they did amount to a technical violation. And we always of course took your word that if you had overlooked a document, you had overlooked it, and that could happen to you, to us, to Mr. Jones, Madam Vidovic, and to everyone in this Tribunal. This document that we're dealing with now seems to be in a category of its own. It goes to the heart of the case. It really goes to the heart of the case. And it's very difficult to explain, although of course we will give you all -- we'll give all due consideration to any statement that you may wish to add. It's very difficult for anyone coming from the Prosecution's side to explain that unfortunately we were not aware of this. Because if it is as simple as you have put it that you could key in the word "Fakovici" and Mr. Jones would have found it on the EDS, equally it should have been so easy for you to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So -- I know it's correct, otherwise I wouldn't be opening my mouth, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I -- if Your Honours please, if it would be easier to understand my submissions, I make it clear there has been a breach of Rule 68 in our failing to provide this document to the Defence. There has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I am glad to hear that being acknowledged at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The problem -- the issue that I was raising was what pressure -- what prejudice was there to the Defence, what could have been -- what could have occurred and what might have occurred in order to lessen the impact of that. And I was just trying to say that it was available to the Defence on EDS and searchable on that particular system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I hope -- and I hope I won't have to repeat this again. There is a big difference for any Defence lawyer between being told, Mr. Jones, Madam Vidovic, this is a document which we are disclosing to you under Rule 68 because it falls within Rule 68 parameters and telling Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, Here I'm giving you three CDs, four CDs, each containing something like 10.000, 20.000 documents, I don't know how many tens if not hundreds of pages, this could be relevant to your case, go through it. The Defence can allow themselves the luxury, if they want to, not to go through all those 30.000, 40.000, 50.000 documents if they think that it's too labourious or that the end result would not really reflect the fruit of the labours. But I can assure that it would take a very responsible and highly responsible Defence lawyer to ignore a document that has been disclosed as a Rule 68 material. So this is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- wait, Mr. Jones, I think you will have every opportunity to deal with this as we go along. So please try to understand, we don't make it more serious than it already looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's far from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I cannot really understand or accept the submission that, you know, this could have been of little consequence because the Defence had it in their ED -- in their CDs, if they had it, because I don't know. Or it was in the EDS, they could have looked it and they could have put all the questions that they would have wished to upon cross-examination when we brought all those Serbian witnesses saying exactly the opposite of what you have in this document. This is very serious. This is very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in fact, I mean I want to know what is your position if it is accepted or it is acknowledged that as a result of the non-disclosure of this as Rule 68 material, questions that could have been put to the Prosecution witnesses were not put by the Defence because they were not aware of this document. I mean, the existence of it in the EDS system, in other words, does not mean that therefore the Defence know -- is aware of it or knows about it or should have been aware of it. They have enough to deal with on a day-to-day basis, let alone to go through tens of thousands of documents to see what is relevant and what is not when they could have easily got it as a Rule 68 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made the submission to you that it appears to be a breach of Rule 68. The -- that would not actually be correct if indeed this document is -- consists of material of a public nature that may be falling under Rule 68. In Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber decision, page 104, paragraph 296, 295, 296, 297, the Appeals Chamber had this to say about documents of a public nature: "Arguably the Prosecution's duty to disclose does not encompass material of a public nature potentially falling under Rule 68, for example," and there refers to the exhibits that were in contention then. The exhibits that were in contention in that appeal were public transcripts of trial proceedings. And they went on to say, the Appeals Chamber said: "However, a distinction should be drawn between material of a public character in the public domain and material reasonably accessible to the Defence. The Appeals Chamber emphasises that unless exculpatory material is reasonably accessible to the accused, namely available to the Defence with the exercise of due diligence, the Prosecution has a duty to disclose the material itself." In the Trial Chamber decision of Blagojevic, Obrenovic, Jokic, and Nikolic, delivered on the 12th of December, 2002, an earlier decision, the same issue, the same sort of issue, arose and there the Trial Chamber said, paragraph 26, page 10: "As the Appeals Chamber has previously held, if exculpatory evidence is known and the evidence is accessible, the Prosecution may be relieved of its obligation to disclose the material under Rule 68." And then it goes on to say: "Rule 68 is not intended to serve as a means through which the Prosecution is forced to replace the Defence in conducting investigations or gathering material." But the operative words are "if" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't follow this without copy. We haven't been notified that authority was going to be relied on, and unless the Prosecution has copies, I don't see how the rest of us are expected to follow legal argument and references to paragraphs when none of us have the decision in front of us. It's a matter of common courtesy to -- if one's going to rely on authority to either provide copies or to give advance notice. Certainly in the UK I wouldn't dream of having legal argument without being told what authorities the Prosecution intends to rely on or having copies in front of me. I have to take Mr. Di Fazio's word for it that this is what is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent right, Mr. Jones. But what's the alternative at this point, stop and get the copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio move on to something else because it's meaningless to refer to authorities which none of us -- I notice that Your Honours don't have the authorities either, so how can any of us follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last thing I would expect us to know is what Mr. Di Fazio is going to come up with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and if I knew you were going cite authority, I could have looked into it. There could be other Appeals Chamber judgements saying completely other things. So it's a pointless exercise in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, in fact, I can assure you that there are subsequent Appeals Chamber decisions that make it clear that with the introductory of new systems, et cetera, the responsibility of the Prosecution under Rule 68 is not diminished. It still remains what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If I can complete my sentence, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. Thank you. I was going to say to you -- I was going to say to you that I wish to complete the submissions tomorrow in order that I might properly research whether or not this web site, this magazine, this article could conceivably come within the description that I mentioned -- the ratio that I mentioned from those two cases. And it's precisely that -- I want to investigate that further because I've only -- the point didn't occur to me until prior to coming into court, and I want to see how well-known this web site is, whether it's a web site, a magazine, what its nature is, and whether it could conceivably come within that description, material within the public domain, so that I might then be in a position to say to you, Right, well, we're fortified in making that submission to you and we persist in it or withdraw it. And that will enable my learned friend to go to Blaskic or go to that particular case. I'm well aware of the need to provide precedents to the other side when making submissions. And I didn't intend, if Your Honours please, to flummox the Defence or to catch them to unawares, and I would think that sort of cheap trick doesn't have any place in this courtroom. So that's why I raised the issue, that's why I mentioned it to you. I have to establish to the satisfaction of the Prosecution that we're in a position to say that this material is within the public domain or it comes from a publication that would permit us to make the submission to you, Right, it's in the public domain. And if it's not, then we have to withdraw that submission and I'm not in a position to do that until I've had a closer look at this publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, as Mr. Jones put it yesterday, this is a matter of extreme urgency, too. And the reason is that this will be the second day this witness is being examined in chief. To be honest with you, I'm not that confident that we will finish with the examination-in-chief today, unless I get a sign from Mr. Jones that I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was planning to, but I doubt it now. I mean, if I might say in that regard, Your Honour, the Prosecution appears to be intending to spend what little time they have finding legal arguments to argue why they haven't violated Rule 68. There's something way more important which we haven't heard anything about from Mr. Di Fazio which is what about this Slobodan Misic case which in 1997 a spokesman of the Prosecutor said they were aware of. Did they get more information from the authorities. Is there anything to disclose to us. I mean, that's -- it's a typically defensive reaction of the Prosecution to try and find some way of arguing that they didn't violate Rule 68. What about a productive approach where they actually look and see was anything obtained from the local authorities and, if so, let's get it to the Defence as quickly as possible. And it's typical of the Prosecution that they haven't considered that very important pressing matter. Instead they're trying to find legal arguments, consulting jurisprudence in the Blaskic case, spending precious time on that, rather than being productive and finding the material which we're asking about. I have further submissions to make, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The spokesman, if Your Honours please, wasn't an OTP spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we can see the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say who the spokesman was, but it would be very bad news for you, Mr. Di Fazio, if it was the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the spokesperson said -- and again, this is nit-picking, Your Honour, in my submission. The spokesperson said that "the Office of the Prosecutor in The Hague knew that the confession of Serbian volunteer, Slobodan Misic, about the crimes in Croatia and Bosnia had been published." Now, that's the point. And he then: "The Office of the Prosecutor in The Hague will contact the competent bodies of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in order to obtain additional information." That's a spokesman of the Tribunal who said that. Now that's what we're interested in, what about this additional information? Surely the Prosecution didn't ignore the confession of someone who said he killed 70 to 80 people and slaughtered them and threw their heads in the Drina. Surely they requested information. Did they get anything? If so, let's see that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing -- before you proceed any further, Mr. Jones, the other thing we are interested in knowing is whether this document -- it seems there's also an inclusion in that it was certainly not disclosed to you under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it disclosed to you -- forget the EDC system, because I'm not really that much interested in that for the time being at least until I've heard further submissions from Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It hasn't been disclosed to us in any form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any form, so it's not even contained in any one of the CDs that reference was made to earlier on this week and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and last week and the week before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And I do have to say, I will make submissions on the EDS, even though I agree with Your Honour that EDS does not relieve the Prosecution of its obligations, and that's clear from Rule 68(i) and (ii), one being without prejudice to the other. We checked the EDS here and in Sarajevo, we check it every two weeks, and we only discovered this document very recently, and we found it with the search criteria we put in. So I simply do not agree with the submission of Mr. Di Fazio that it's been there since 2004, but I don't want to get into that because I see another possible tactic by the Prosecution to get diverted into that issue, and that isn't the issue. The issue isn't even really -- it's disclosure of these documents but it's also the Misic case. And to make that clear, it's two documents and a whole case on what inquiries were made. Even though we are a small team - we are essentially the team you see here today - we do check thousands of documents and we were not aware of this document until two weeks ago, and we check EDS religiously and regularly. I have other submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Should I move on to those? I don't know if Mr. Di Fazio is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I would close the debate today, as much as I can, and then leave the last part --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my suggestion or -- and we are in agreement on this, is that you proceed with your submissions which may shed more light on matters that Mr. Di Fazio may ultimately wish to address tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- then in the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His conclusive intervention, we hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for that opportunity, because I do think this raises fundamental issues about the approach of the Prosecution in this case. And I have to say I think it's a typically defensive and unrepentant submission by the Prosecution which we've heard this morning. There was nothing like a mea culpa until the Prosecution realised from indications from Your Honour that some sort of a mea culpa might be in order. And then very quickly Mr. Di Fazio said instead that it appeared to be a breach, it wasn't necessarily a breach, and that he is going to see if he can find legal arguments overnight to argue why it isn't a Rule 68 breach. I don't think that's a particularly repentant or productive approach to this issue, and it's typical and it's endemic and it's why we're having such problems with Rule 68, because the Prosecution has this defensive attitude to Rule 68. And the moment we raise an issue like this, they seek to immediately blame us, to say the Defence had access. That's a typical reaction, I have to say, from their part. They haven't said, We've looked into changing our procedures, we've appointed a Rule 68 officer, we've made urgent inquiries to see whether we have anything on the Slobodan Misic case. That's what we expected, that's what we deserve, frankly, in this case, that's what our client deserves, that the Prosecution go off and look and see what is out on there Slobodan Misic and get it to us pretty quickly. That's what all of us deserve, and we didn't get it this morning from Mr. Di Fazio. As to a couple of preliminary matters, in a way, arising from his submissions. He's obviously seeking to suggest, Mr. Di Fazio, that this article -- first of all, this publication Focus is well-known, it's like Time magazine or The Guardian. Well, frankly, we've never heard of it. I think it's thoroughly obscure. In any event, Focus, let's remember, is Annex C. Annex A is utterly obscure. That's certainly not something which -- a publication or a document which we're particularly familiar with. So to try and stretch this to say this was in the public domain, well, I suppose, ultimately everything is somehow in the public domain. But to anticipate his argument and to perhaps fire a broadside, in a sense, that it's a waste of time to seek to suggest these documents were in the public domain, but if need be, we'll get into that, but as I say, I think that would be thoroughly unproductive. Much more fundamentally, Your Honours, I'm very worried and I think Your Honours should be very worried about the Prosecution's approach to Rule 68. In my submission, their response, initial response of Mr. Di Fazio seeking to argue that these documents weren't exculpatory shows that in fact they don't understand their case and they don't understand our case, and it's very dangerous for this case that they don't and it's very dangerous for Rule 68 disclosure that they don't understand the case. And that's the reason why we haven't been getting much Rule 68 material. Not because it doesn't exist but because the Prosecution doesn't know what its case is and what our defence is, and I intend to illustrate that. The Prosecution don't seem to be aware that their witnesses have been consistently saying that there were merely village guards in these villages, that there was no VRS presence, there were no volunteers, that there was no necessity for attacking villages. They don't seem to be aware that their case, their whole case, is based on there being a Muslim army with a unified command structure and that unified command structure being under Naser Oric. And it's actually very rare -- and this is another point which I'm going to raise separately -- it's very rare the Prosecution puts their case to our witnesses, and it's a matter which I'm going to insist on at some stage. It's very rare that they do, as they should do under the Rules, under Rule 90(H)(ii). On one occasion Mr. Di Fazio did, and these are his words: "I suggest that these groups --" This is from the transcript page 10899, 13th September, 2005: "I suggest that these groups all converged in places like Jagodnja and Joseva and Kravica, these district groups, because there was a central command structure, a central command structure of which you're aware and a central command structure who was headed at the top by Mr. Oric. Would you agree or not with that proposition?" That's their case, and that's what Article 7(3) depends on, a central command structure, with Mr. Naser Oric at its head. And here we have documents saying there was no Muslim army, there were just civilians in this very area, in the Fakovici area. And if the Prosecution doesn't realise that that affects their case, then that's very worrying. That's troubling for us and it should be troubling for Your Honours. The Prosecution almost appear to think that the case is: Did Naser Oric set fire to houses? Did he as an individual go around committing crimes? And if they find maybe a document which says that he didn't, then maybe they'll consider that exculpatory. But that's not the case. The case is based on command responsibility. It's: Did Naser Oric's subordinates commit these crimes? Did he know or should he have known about those crimes? And in terms of whether he should have known, there's jurisprudence, I'm not going to cite jurisprudence, I'll just list the factors which have been mentioned: The number of illegal acts, the type of illegal acts, the scope of illegal acts, the time during which the illegal acts occurred, the number and type of troops involved, the logistics involved, the geographical location of the acts, the widespread occurrence of the acts, the tactical tempo of operations, the modus operandi of similar illegal acts, the offices and staff involved, the location of the commander at the time. That's from Celebici trial judgement. All of that is relevant simply to knowledge. And then we have under Article 7(3) necessary and reasonable measures which a commander could take. And there's a great deal which is relevant to what a commander can do about alleged crimes committed by his subordinates. And we've been saying this is a time when there were massacres; expulsions of Muslims; appalling danger from the Serbs, that they would break through the lines and massacre the civilians; starvation; imminent genocide. That's the picture we portrayed right from the start, and Your Honours will of course remember the opening speech and those were highlighted at the top as themes which we would develop. Because of course in any sensible point of view, and I trust that this Tribunal and certainly this Trial Chamber has enough -- has sufficient common sense to consider that it's relevant to the priorities a commander is going to have if he's operating in a situation of such appalling danger, whether, if he even knew of these crimes, which we deny and we've said there's been no evidence of our client knowing of burning and what not, but is he going to investigate a possible burning of a house on some hillside when there's a risk of women and children being massacred? We've made that case time and again. And if the Prosecution doesn't realise that the fact of facing this constant attack from a merciless enemy is relevant to that and it's exculpatory if there is material which shows that there was this ruthless attack from the Serbs all along the Drina in this time period. But the Prosecution -- they'll see material like that and they'll say, well, it's not relevant because, I don't know, it doesn't concern the burning of an individual house. That's not the law, it's not customary law, it's not the practice of this Tribunal. I trust, as I say, that the Trial Chamber will not erect some ridiculous standard according to which a commander has absolutely the same duties irrespective of the circumstances under which he's operating. Under military necessity, I submit that the Prosecution has completely misunderstood military necessity. If you've reviewed, as we have, military manuals on customary law and wanton destruction, the emphasise is on military targets and whether an area is militarised, because of course you can expect a lot of destruction from fierce fighting in a danger -- in an area which is militarised with troops and artillery, et cetera. And if you look at photographs of Stalingrad and Berlin and Coventry after war, you'll see most homes have a lot of damage. That's typical of a militarised zone. And that's why we're showing, in case the Prosecution hasn't realised this, that there were battalions of soldiers in these villages, that there was artillery, that there were volunteers who had committed terrible crimes and who were very dangerous, that there were minefields. That's the military necessity to attack because these murderous attacks had been carried out by Serbs from these places. So we turn to this article in which a volunteer based in Fakovici, a village named in our indictment and portrayed as a simple hillside, rustic community, according to the Prosecution, he's admitted to mass murder, 70 to 80 people on his own account, and thousands of others, killing women, killing people who were simply going for food, throwing their bodies into the Drina, that he's assisted by units from Bratunac, and that it wasn't a real Muslim army. That's why I find -- at the outset I was horrified to hear the Prosecution try to wrangle out of that being exculpatory. Surely any sensible Prosecutor would say this is a terrible mistake, this is very exculpatory, it's a terrible error on our part and we'll do everything we can to remedy this mistake. Not a word of that from Mr. Di Fazio, you'll notice. And so if the Prosecution doesn't realise what's exculpatory and what isn't and continues to insist on their approach and then when found out -- they've been found out in this instance, to be reactive and defensive and try to find authority which will maybe offer them an escape route, then the only solution is for Your Honours to direct them in no uncertain terms that they're to disclose to us what is exculpatory, and to tell them what's exculpatory because they don't seem to know, they don't seem to understand what damages their case and what supports our version of events. So, Your Honours, those are my submissions. And I would just add, Your Honour at one point said that you feared that -- or the risk that at the end of this trial it would be half-baked because there would have been nondisclosure of material which would then come to light after the trial. Well, there is a very real risk of that in this case, and at the very best, that would result in successful appeal if, in the sad event of our client being convicted of any charges. But at worst, it would result in a miscarriage of justice, which I hope not only the Chamber but the Prosecution, the Prosecution should also be concerned to avoid a miscarriage of justice. I would also just note in this regard that until very recently, until the Rule 98 bis, there were still charges of plunder in the indictment against Naser Oric. Certainly the Prosecution wasn't about to drop those charges, even though the only evidence was of civilians stealing food, if it can be called stealing. They didn't disclose the document to us either at that stage when those charges were still live, even though the article speaks about starving Muslims who were desperate for food. So frankly, Your Honour, those are my submissions. There is -- as I say, the motion is concerned with documents, yes, those two documents, but it is concerned with the Slobodan Misic case, which we know the Prosecution knew about in 1997, so I don't know what business the Prosecution has trying to shift the date forward to 2002, 2003. Again, very indicative, in my submission, that rather than facing the fact that they knew of this in 1997, they tried to suggest they only knew of it later. There must have been inquiries. The Prosecution surely would be interested in a case of such gravity. There must have been inquiries. We want to know what the results of those inquiries were, what information was received, and we need to receive them immediately. Finally, on prejudice, there is enormous prejudice, obviously, as Your Honour has grasped. We've had witnesses from Fakovici who said, no, we were simply the minding our own business. The Muslims left their villages, they didn't want to live with us anymore, they wanted to live in the woods. If we could have presented documents like this to them and said, well, look, what about this chap, Slobodan Misic, does that change what you say? Perhaps they would have said, well, actually, to be perfectly honest, this stuff did go on and in fact here are some examples which I can give, and, yes, you're right, this and this happened. They might have given completely different evidence, it could have been a completely different trial if we had documents like this at the beginning. So again, Prosecution shouldn't try and wrangle out of that. Unless I can assist further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I'm not going to say much more, Mr. Di Fazio. I don't know if you still insist in postponing until tomorrow your final submissions on what you hope to transpire by then, that we're talking of a document which was in the public domain, or whether you want to close your submissions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I would like to ascertain that, make our inquiries about that, and see if that submission is to be developed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If it is capable of development and the Prosecution feels that it's covered by those two cases, then we wouldn't be using any escape routes. But I would like to make those inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say two things. I neglected to mention one manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You'll recall also seeing Annex B in which you'll see that we were asking specifically for documents from Fakovici. So it's not just EDS issue, it's the fact that we've explicitly been putting the Prosecution on notice that we want any material relating to Fakovici, any material relating to killings of Muslims. Secondly, just on Mr. Di Fazio's point, he can cite jurisprudence if he wants, I hope it will be Appeals Chamber jurisprudence, because of course there's no binding precedent from Trial Chamber jurisprudence, but in my submission, the Rules control. And Rule 68 is clear and Rule 68(ii) also is clear in that without prejudice to paragraph (i), the Prosecution should make available to the Defence, in electronic form, the various collections, but that's without prejudice to the obligation to disclose material in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution. And this is in their actual knowledge, so the EDS is absolutely -- is a red herring. And finally, I really would regret it if Mr. Di Fazio spends time on -- researching case law when there is a much more urgent, pressing issue which we frankly demand to have an answer to, which is what do the Prosecution know about the Misic case, what information have they received? It doesn't have to be documents. Rule 68 is broad enough to include any results they've had from those inquiries, and we absolutely require to have an answer on that matter by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. One moment, please, and we'll discuss among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the discussion is adjourned until tomorrow on this. In the meantime, Mr. Di Fazio, just -- and Mr. Wubben and the rest of the team, the other concern that has been raised by Mr. Jones, namely, his anxiety -- I wouldn't say his suspicion that you have other case related to Misic -- other information related to Misic. I will be more moderate in my -- in the words that I choose. His anxiety to make sure that there is no further material -- Rule 68 material to be disclosed arising from this Misic affair, that you use the time that you have between today and tomorrow to research that, too. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's already underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We discussed a little bit whether we should require you to come back with the information on whether the document's public domain or not public domain, in writing, but I suggested forget that. You do it orally tomorrow at quarter past 2.00, when we reconvene tomorrow, and you use the time, rather than writing down formal documents, that you use it to research properly the archives that you have on this area. Let me finish by making an observation. You realise that throughout this case, since its inception, we have had several instances of complaints from the Defence, sometimes arising out of Rule 66, sometimes arising out of Rule 68, and we have always dealt with them. Sometimes they were dealt with in a very practical manner in the courtroom itself following a kind of entente between the two parties, an understanding more. And you will also understand that this kind of complaints arise in every case. In Brdjanin, for example, I had several instances of alleged violations, some were of little momentum, like some have been also in this case, without great consequences; some pretty serious. And when it was a pretty serious mistake on the part of the Prosecution - and pretty serious mistakes do happen - Ms. Korner, Ms. Joanna Korner, it goes to her credit, one of the best counsel I have come across in my career, would stand up and say, "Your Honours, I don't know how to address you, this is a gross mistake that we have made. Know by faith it was just an oversight, we are sorry, and we are at your disposal. Whatever needs to be done will be done." But trying to take a defensive approach when it may be blatantly -- not just an oversight but maybe something more than that, is -- can call for very serious consequences after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's why -- if Your Honour pleases, that's why I've asked for this time to go and assess whether or not we will maintain that latter submission to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But again --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it is defensive because until a couple of years ago when you had the EDS system, et cetera, and it made changes to Rule 68, including the knowledge of and without the knowledge of, depending on whether those words were to be retained, et cetera, the complaint on the part of the Defence -- not the Defence in this case, Defence teams in every case, used to be, Listen, you, Madam Prosecutor, you have rendered Rule 68(i) as a monster. Because instead of sitting down and distinguish and separate what is truly Rule 68 material from what is not, you're just sending us bundles and bundles and bundles of documents on the pretext that they are Rule 68 material, and then we have to go through the humongous exercise of identifying where the exculpatory material is. That used to be the complaint. So the approach of the Prosecution at the time was: When in doubt, do -- not when in doubt don't, when in doubt, do. And you used to disclose everything, even if the -- you had ambivalence as to whether it was exculpatory or not. But the Prosecution never took the risk. So it becomes a little bit -- very difficult to digest at this point in time now saying -- because first -- you know, now we need to see whether it was public domain or not because, you know, an Appeals Chamber said that when it is public domain -- of course I hope you draw a distinction between a transcript of proceedings and a newspaper or a magazine somewhere. I mean, they may have written something about the war in Bosnia at the time in the Maltese papers, and they are public domain. Would you expect Mr. Jones -- or if they had a Maltese on that team to go through the Maltese papers as well to see whether there was anything exculpatory at the time. CNN news, BBC news, they are almost occurring on a daily basis. I'm sure that there is, if one were to look into those, a lot of exculpatory material for this case and other cases. But come on, are we talking of public domain material? If you know about them, and if you have them in your records, as you seem to have had this for a long time, and it is Rule 68 material and it cannot but be Rule 68 material, I'm not saying -- I'm not deciding now that it is definitely and by no other means Rule 68 material; that will be decided later, obviously. But looking -- looking at it, you shouldn't have too much doubt. And if you don't -- shouldn't have too much doubt today, really you must come up with some really good justification why you - when I say "you" it's not you, Mr. Di Fazio, please don't misunderstand me - why you weren't aware of it in 2002, 2003, 2004, and until we started the case in October 2004. And it does -- I agree with Mr. Jones, it does go to the heart of the case. It really goes to the heart of the case. I've never spoken so openly on any issue or on any document that was contested on by the Defence on Rule 66 or on Rule 68 as I am doing today. And the reason is to try and avert undesirable consequences. I mean, it's -- it's problematic. This document presents the Trial Chamber with a lot of problems, with a lot of -- and I hope you understand what I am saying. So we'll continue the discussion tomorrow. Usher will now please escort the witness into the courtroom. Has he been told that we would be -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Does Your Honour intend to break at 3.45?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I be excused at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the least we see of you between today and tomorrow, the better it will be, because we assume you will be researching further into the -- into the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your absence will be a good sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm glad Your Honours said "the archives" rather than the case law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- by the way, because I forgot to tell you, today we will be sitting like yesterday, until 7.00. So there will be two breaks, one within 20 minutes from now, and the other one at quarter to 6.00, quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- good afternoon to you, Mr. Alic, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please accept the apologies of the Trial Chamber for calling you an hour and a quarter after you were supposed to start giving evidence. The reason is we had serious procedural business to transact, which of course doesn't have to do with you. I mean, I want to put your mind at rest that you were not involved in the debate that we had here. And we are now in a position to continue. Mr. Jones will continue with his examination-in-chief. I don't think we will finish today, but there is still hope that we will be able to finish with you by Friday -- by the end of Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And apologies from me, too, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when we left off we were discussing the situation in Jagodnja and Joseva in early October 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you told us there were daily attacks by Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention now on the 4th of October, 1992. You've told us there were daily attacks. Was there an attack on that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was this an infantry attack or an artillery attack or both?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of October, 1992, there was shelling during the day. As for the night between the 4th and the 5th, there was an incursion by a group of Serb soldiers. Between the villages of Jagodnja and Josevo, there was a forest-keeper's hut there which had not been torched previously. There were refugees from Joseva staying there whose houses had been torched. That night three Zolja missiles were fired on this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned an incursion by a group of Serb soldiers. Do you know from which direction they came?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what the people who were in the area, or rather, in the house told me, the group had come from the direction of Fakovici, or rather, had withdrawn to the Jezero area, to sum it up, the Fakovici area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've mentioned that three Zolja missiles were fired on this building, the building of the forest-keeper.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What happened to that building?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building was made of stone. It had a stone wall about 60 centimetres thick. There wasn't much damage that the Zoljas -- Zolja missiles could cause. One of those - this is something that we saw later on - hit the roof directly. There was a powerful explosion, but there wasn't much damage to the house at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, what were you doing at the time of this attack -- or rather, where were you, firstly?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a part of the village of Hasanovici. The distance is one to one and a half kilometres. I was there with the wounded who had been injured over the previous days. My duty was to keep an eye on those people and to dress their wounds on a daily basis and whatever else they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on the occasion of this attack, between the 4th and the 5th of October, 1992, were there many wounded who you had to treat?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this hut there were about three people who were wounded, wounded as a result of the explosion that I mentioned, because the explosion had been so powerful. People were afraid. They were trying to escape. And on their way out, they were injured. These people eventually made it to the village of Hasanovici. They escaped. And when they arrived, I dressed their wounds. I administered first aid to the people who arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did help arrive at any stage from outside your village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening the shelling on Josevi continued. In the early hours there was an exchange of fire. There was infantry combat between Joseva and Priselaca which is where the Serb soldiers, I'm talking about the next morning, launched another attack against Joseva. At this point in time, a man from Joseva came up to me, to where I was in Hasanovici, and told me that should I so chose I was free to join him on his way to Bradva, that is, Joseva and on to Priselaca. When I got there --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Stop there for a second. I think we should mark that on the map, the places you've just mentioned. If you could be shown the map, D827. Yes, first you mentioned a place I think called Bredala [phoen]. If you could just mention the two places you said a moment ago and then mark them, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will show you on the map my whereabouts at the time and then I'll take one thing at a time. This is Hasanovici, a village that had not been torched, the dozen houses that were there. Then I headed for Bradva --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, can you please mark that with an H, Hasanovici.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, and please continue.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked Bradva with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And then Priselaca -- Priselaca I think you mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not a village, it's just a place, Priselaca. This is the location, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to come back to your movements in second. But first you mentioned artillery was shooting I think you said on Joseva. Do you know the direction from which the artillery was shooting?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the accounts of the people who were there, it was from the direction of Fakovici and to a much lesser extent from the direction of Bijeli Kamen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say from the accounts of the people who were there, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the group who were observing the area, who were carrying out reconnaissance in the Joseva area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So did they see that the artillery was firing from the direction of Fakovici or that it was actually -- did they actually see the artillery pieces in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could not see anything from Priselaca that was coming from Fakovici but you could hear anything that was going on. If you have a mortar, a 120-millimetre or an 80-millimetre mortar, when it fires, you can hear it the same way you can hear a missile. You can tell the direction. But from Bijeli Kamen, if you used binoculars, you could see where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And now going back to the map and explaining your movements, can you first explain why you were moving in this direction, what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a man came along and asked me to join him on his way there. There had been fighting between the Serb soldiers and the group of people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So why did he ask you along?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was the nurse, so that if anyone was wounded I was there to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could you say -- could you mark where you went from the place you've located -- you've marked with P. Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I reached Priselaca there was a group of people there that I was not familiar with. I asked them why they were there, and they said they were there to help us. I understood that they were from Kragljivoda and other villages, too. There were plenty of civilians there moving in that direction, in the vicinity of Priselaca. We headed for Radijevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you stop there for a minute. You mentioned people from Kragljivoda who said they had come to help. Was that the first time help had come from other villages or had it happened before?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first time that people arrived in our village in order to help us with defending or to offer help against the attacks that we were being subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And before you move on to Radijevici, were there civilians there in that area on that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my estimate - and you must understand that there was a lot of confusion at the time - there were many hundreds in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just to fix the time, you were talking about the 4th of October or the 5th of October now?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And what were the civilians doing there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilians arrived. They heard about the shelling, about the firing. The civilians were going wherever there was shooting in the hope that they would be able to lay their hands on some food or whatever they could use to feed themselves, their family, get some clothing, perhaps, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And at this stage, on this day, did the Muslims in Jagodnja and Joseva still only have five or six rifles or did you have more at this stage?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had more. We got more weapons, so at this time we had between 20 and 30 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you explain some of the ways in which you got those weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, during the attack where we put up resistance in Jagodnja we managed to seize some of the rifles that the Serb soldiers had left behind. There were a lot of people coming from the neighbouring villages to our village, from Visegrad, from Zepa, from Krusev Do and other places, too. They would bring weapons because they had no food to survive, to feed their families. So we helped those people and they realised what our situation was. We had some sort of an exchange. They would leave their weapons behind and we would give them food in return. There were other people, too, who would come from wherever, I'm not sure where they were coming from. They would stay a fortnight or so, and some of these people carried rifles and wanted food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And those rifles, were they given to any specific single person or were they shared among the people in the village as a whole?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one in particular was given a rifle, saying this rifle is for you; it was for the general purpose of defending the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it was shared among people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I stopped you when you were going towards Radijevici. Did you see anything in particular in Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was the so-called counter-attack on Radijevici. I joined the fighters myself. And on the way to Radijevici about 100 or 200 metres further down the road we came across mines. There were about three mines that had been laid in the forest at the point where we were supposed to cross. We removed those mines -- actually, there was a person from my village who was part of the group and he was successful in removing these mines. After that, another group came, a group that was to our left, and they ran into a minefield, the mines killing four people instantly. There was a zigzag pattern to the mines. Some of them were land-mines and the other mines were a kind that we refer to as cans.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, I have a question in that regard. Secondly - and I was just waiting for the interpretation - land-mines and others referred to as cans. What are those cans? How are they activated?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see those myself. I didn't see what they were like, but they're activated as soon as someone steps on them and then they go off.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are there also trip-wire mines that are activated by someone triggering a string or wire?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These are not the same kind. Trip-wire is the one where you have wire, but they're visible usually, and then you have some sort of a wire and someone trips over it. We had removed those, but these land-mines, these mines you can't see because they're dug into the ground and you can't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. There might be a slight misinterpretation there. But that was the point, really, there were also these trip-wire mines in the area which you mentioned that you deactivated. Just one question before we break. You mentioned that you joined the fighters. How many people were in this group of fighters, or how many of these fighters were there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my group there were between 10 and 15 fighters, people from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we can break there if that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before the break, Mr. Alic, you mentioned these 10 to 15 fighters. Were any of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did all or any of them have weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most people had weapons except for me and two other people who were with me. They were carrying stretchers and they didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say "most people," you're referring to most among those 10 to 15 of the fighters?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were describing how you were in Radijevici. Do you know a place called Radijevici Potok?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he mentioned it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you go to or did you see Radijevici Potok?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the place where the mines were and where those people on the other side had been killed, from there you can see Radijevici Potok with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see anything going on in that area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that place, Radijevici Potok, we noticed that there was a lorry and Serb soldiers were getting off. And there was some extra weapons there. I think it was the mortars that they were setting up there. And we noticed across the river Drina there was a boat crossing over from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what that boat was doing or could you see what that boat was doing?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were ferrying something. I wasn't able to see what exactly it was, but there was some cargo. And you could also spot people on the boat. And as to there was anything else, I don't know, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as this vehicle was concerned the Serb soldiers got off, this lorry, what sort of a vehicle was it, what sort of a lorry?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned how there was some mines, and I think you mentioned you were able to deactivate some. Now, aside from the mines which the people you described stepped on, were any other mines activated?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those four soldiers were killed, there was a great deal of shooting and the shooting was coming from the village of Radijevici. You could hear shooting alongside these houses which were just below the forest in Radijevici. So the shooting started towards where we were and where those people were killed. So mines -- certain mines that were below our positions were activated as well. Those were special mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. I just want to clarify that. You mentioned there was shooting --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trip-wire mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Shooting alongside these houses which were just in the forest of Radijevici. What village or hamlet were these houses in that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses are below the forest, Novi Radijevici, and that connects to Radijevici Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that part of Radijevici or is that some other place?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the Radijevici itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've mentioned -- you said these houses were in Radijevici and then you described shooting alongside these houses. Where in fact was the shooting coming from in relation to the houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Radijevici, that is to say, shells were landing there from the direction of Fakovici. And there was a lot of shooting and shooting started from all sides. So there was so much noise in that valley that it was impossible to even reach any conclusions as to where the shooting was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said "from the village of Radijevici." The witness said that the shooting came from the village of Radijevici, from those houses, and I don't see it in the transcript, from the houses in the village of Radijevici. 16.24.00 he said "from the village of Radijevici, from those houses" and then he went on to talk about shells, and I didn't see the mention of houses in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. I think you better verify that. It certainly doesn't show up in the transcript for sure and that does make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, did you say the shooting came from the houses in the village of Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you were also saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if Your Honours will permit me to look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you seem to be suggesting that the shooting activated certain mines. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And do you know who was shooting from those houses in Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
